utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I understand both parties have matters to raise. The Chamber has a couple of matters, and the first one is that the Defence teams, both Defence teams are ordered to file the list of witnesses to be called on behalf of the Defence should the Rule 98 bis judgement establish that there is a case to answer, and this list is to contain all the information required pursuant to Rule 65 ter (G)(i) and is to be filed together with a list of exhibits pursuant to Rule 65 ter (G)(ii). In view of scheduling of the breaks in this case as already announced, the Trial Chamber requires this information to be provided no later than Friday, 17th October 2008. The Chamber is in the process now of filing its decision in relation to the motion of 8th September to substitute VG-42 for VG-85 and VG-64 for VG-71. That motion is granted, but the Prosecution should note that according to its terms, the earliest date for testimony is the 27th of October, and the reason for that is to give the Defence time to prepare. Now, who is first, Mr. Groome or -- Mr. Groome, you have matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, as the case has progressed I see one of my responsibilities as trying to in view of prosecuting the case most efficiently is always re-evaluating the witnesses that are on the list. One of the witnesses we sought to add on the 8th of September 2008 is Witness VG-137. He's a convicted Serb perpetrator. A statement was recorded on video over the summer, but it was not until last week that we actually had the transcript. Now after reviewing the full transcript and fully considering the security implications that this witness's family may face as a result of testifying in a case that -- and these security implications have nothing to do with the Defence of the particular accused in this case but just the general security concerns that they have, I believe it is in the interest of justice that I not call the witness at this stage. So I will be withdrawing the -- our request to add VG-137. Of course I apologise to Defence counsel and court staff, legal officers that may have expended efforts in this regard already, but I believe it's consistent with my duties to keep re-evaluating the witness list and reducing it where possible. Your Honour, last week when I filed the -- the witness schedule for this week I mentioned the witness Zehra Turjacanin, and there was a question mark about whether she would be available to testify this Thursday. She has arrived in The Hague and it is our intention to call her this Thursday. I do have one request of the Chamber and that is I think it is preferable for her if her testimony begins and concludes on a single day. I think it may cause her some problems to be worrying overnight. I know that we originally had requested and were granted three hours to examine her. It would be my request and my intention to reduce my examination of her to an hour and 45 minutes, and I would request if we could begin her testimony on Thursday morning and conclude it Thursday afternoon. So I'd ask the Chamber to consider that, that even if we should be ahead of schedule on Wednesday that we do allow her just to begin her testimony on Thursday -- Thursday morning. Now, Your Honour, this week we are scheduled to call two experts and they have they devoted a significant portion of their professional pursuits to what happened in Visegrad. Pursuant to the Chamber's earlier ruling we are intending this week to produce these witnesses, tender their prior testimony and reports and make them available for cross-examination. In preparing them for their testimony, it appears that there may be some benefit to asking them some brief additional evidence. For example, as a result of the assertion of an alibi defence, we have called several witnesses to rebut that alibi. Some of those witnesses in their evidence refer to killings of other named people. Ms. Tabeau examined the available data sources for these names and is able to provide information regarding the date which has been recorded as their death. Now, the dates are often approximate and are determined by information provided by family members as to when they last saw the victim. However, given this caveat, they do provide corroboration of the fact that these victims were killed as well as an approximate date. She has also examined her underlying data sources and generated a table of victims named in the indictment and is able to provide similar information about when they are believed to have been reported missing. She has also in preparation for her testimony prepared a PowerPoint presentation that succinctly summarises her report and shows in graphic format her primary conclusions. Among these is a graph that shows the dates when there was a statistical spike in the killings in Visegrad. I believe it would be useful for the Chamber to see this presentation and hear her explanation. I anticipate that both of these matters could be dealt with in approximately 50 minutes, so I'd ask the Chamber to consider whether the Prosecution would be allowed to -- to spend approximately 50 minutes inquiring from Ms. Tabeau on these other matters. Similarly, Dr. John Clark, who with his colleagues performed the examination of the remains found in Slap arrived in The Hague over the weekend. His Vasiljevic testimony has been -- will be admitted pursuant to a decision of the Chamber. Many of the remains that he examined have now been identified. Three of them are named victims in the indictment. The Prosecution is therefore requesting approximately 10 minutes to examine Dr. Clark and have him talk about the specific files, the specific autopsy reports with respect to three cases that he conducted that have to do with named victims in the indictment. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, your mike.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would you please clarify, Mr. Groome, the position of Ms. Tabeau. Is she down to testify it the same day as -- as Zehra Turjacanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I had indicated an earlier time because she works in the building I've identified her a person who can be called on short notice should a gap arise. In the filing that we made last Thursday, we identified that we would call her today because we anticipated that even we would be ahead of schedule today because of the Chamber's deferral of the decision of the VG-42 who was originally intended to be today. So she is available to give her evidence today, and she would be the second witness that we would call this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. First to respond to the issues which is raised by my learned friend Mr. Groome. We do not object, of course, that witness Zehra Turjacanin will appear in one day so no objection related to that. We kindly request the whole material from OTP related to the VG-137. Maybe could be useful for Defence. We don't know yet that. And I would like to raise some other issues. One of that is admission of exhibit which we used with last witness, Nurko Dervisevic. That is the pseudonym sheet. We forgot to request admission of that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll admit that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 2D18 under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And what I would like to raise is as follows as the main, main issue is related to upcoming witnesses, namely on Friday late afternoon we were informed from the OTP that in our lockers are the new disclosure related to the witnesses for this week, so on Saturday we checked and we received 1.304 pages related to the witness Ewa Tabeau, 1.004 pages related to John Clark, and 284 pages related to Witness Mirsad Tokaca. On Sunday afternoon we received additional disclosure material and in that disclosure we found exhibit which the OTP intends to use with that witness, that is the CV, updated CV of Ewa Tabeau, but in all this material and in the previous material we haven't got received data sources for the Ewa Tabeau expert report related to Visegrad. That means population census from 1991 and from 1997 voters register mainly because Ms. Tabeau quoted in her expertise that these sources are reliable and relevant to our objectives. On Friday morning we were invited from OTP to -- by e-mail to contact them and to review all material related to that witness, but this morning when we requested that material, the basic material for that report, we received information that this material is under the Rule 70. It is quite confusing for us, because in our opinion that material cannot fall under that Rule because Rule 70(a) specifies that reports, memoranda or other internal documents prepared by a party, its assistants or representatives in connection with the investigation or the preparation of the case are not subject to disclosure or notification under those rules, but the present situation we did not request any previously mentioned documents. We simply requested material requested by public institution which is essential and forms the basis of the expert report. We cannot be prepared for cross-examination without that material because it is clearly quoted in that material that is the base for that report. We needed that material for effective preparation. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, did I want to inform the Court that of course doubling with Mr. Cepic, that was one of our main concerns and we did file a motion to bar the testimony of the Prosecution expert based on the late disclosure and the refusal to tender the Rule 70 materials in accordance with the Rules and the procedures of the court. I don't think the motion has come out yet because we filed it -- we were writing it this morning, Your Honour, and so that's what basically we focused on this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, I want to say one thing. I don't intend to devote a lot of time on this because there are other ways of settling these issues. For example, Mr. Cepic, if you believe something is not Rule 70, then you can file a motion to that effect and it will be determined. But I would like to hear Mr. Groome on the late disclosures of documentation which appears to be very voluminous, over a thousand pages, and briefly also on the other matter raised by Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm asking Mr. Van Hooydonk to get the precise numbers. At the end of last week both of these experts had done work in the former Yugoslavia. We disclosed material that was disclosable under Rule 66 and Rule 68. We then sent a letter towards the end of last week saying look, there's this whole other body of material, it's not disclosable under Rule 66 in that it's not a prior statement of this witness related to anything, to Visegrad or anything to do with this case and there's nothing in that's exculpatory, but they have worked in this area and they've done much work in other parts of Bosnia and Croatia and the former Yugoslavia. So we said to them there's no -- there's no confidentiality in those documents. If you want access to those documents we will provide that access to those documents, and I believe Defence counsel did want access to those documents. I'm asking Mr. Van Hooydonk now to get me the precise figures about what, if any, portion of this was material that we were required to disclose and what portion of it was material we offered as a courtesy to Defence counsel even though it was not disclosable under the Rules and as soon as I have that information I can report that to the Chamber. With respect to the other matter raised by Mr. Cepic, what's in issue are a very large database or two databases of voter registration records of entire country of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It actually refers to 9.5 million individuals records, each of those records containing 50 to 60 different variables or data points within it. So it's in the billions of -- of -- on the magnitude of the information that's contained in there. Ewa Tabeau has never provided this before in another case. She received this pursuant to some Rule 70 agreement. I'm not sure who that is with and I can investigate that for Your Honours. She has stated that it has happened in the past where Defence teams have hired their own demographer and she has made available the database up in our office where they can look and do checks on the database. If that is what Defence counsel is requesting, that is something that could be arranged. I think it's a bet tangential to this issue in that this case, unlike the other cases where Ewa Tabeau has testified such as the Srebrenica cases where the actual victims that the accused were charged with where part of that proof is established with her records, the Prosecution in this particular case is not seeking to establish that any of the individuals killed here were killed as a result or relying -- or we're not relying on Ewa Tabeau's assessment of this database but we can make it available to the Defence. If they want, Ms. Tabeau tells us that it would take about a week to set up a room, the computers, and again I'm not sure if Defence counsel appreciate exactly what they're asking, but it's not the type of material that those of us who are untrained in demography can sit down and make use of. It's something that does require a demographic expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, just briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just briefly. Thank you very much for this opportunity. We just requested material related to Visegrad municipality which was the base for this -- for this report, nothing more than that. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't intend to determine any of these matters now. If a party has an application to make to the Chamber then it can make that application. Please call the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, I still have a preliminary matter separate from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have another preliminary matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Please, sir, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: To be honest I don't know where to begin, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That sounds very ominous, Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, it is, because I'm raising right now an effective assistance of counsel and I do that because I had to become introspective but the comment you gave me on Friday, the reputation of misrepresenting the facts or the evidence cut very deeply. I took it very seriously, because the last thing I want is this Tribunal to somehow not respect my integrity. I took it very seriously because I take this process very seriously. I entered into this process very seriously, and when you do public defender work at any time, you don't get to choose your client, you don't get to choose your case, and you don't make up the facts but you do the best you can every time, and what I'd like to think is that this process -- and we have raised submissions to the counsel with regards to how difficult it has been to prepare this case in the time-frame ordered by the Court, and I hate to complain all the time so we don't complain every time we can, but what you said cut me very deeply, Your Honour, and I want to first explain to you in a bit what it takes for us to do what we do every day and what we've been asked to do despite the fact that I've only been lead counsel since June and I didn't get any help before this point in time. So basically I've been the lone counsel, even as co-counsel since February of this case and there were 50 submissions in this case in July when we should be just tearing apart these witnesses and putting them back together again. The witness list has been remade and retwisted around and now reformulated. New witnesses who've never been heard of before are being added. 42 is being substituted. We spent the weekend writing our responses, Your Honour, and you've made your decision first thing in the morning on Monday, even though our decision to -- our option to reply to that is not even done. And it makes me feel like I'm wasting my time because to be honest, Your Honour, if you've convicted my client based on 63 we should go home. We should go home, because at that point in time I think this Court has enough at least in the State of Florida to kill the man. And so the fact is, Your Honour, is I have 21 counts all involving individual murders or atrocities of one kind or another and then they're back-dooring persecution through rape victims under the auspice of alibis? I'm sorry, Your Honour, it's not an alibi unless the witness comments on the date in question. I want to make an oral argument not to allow the witness today because they tender them under alibi; yet this is a back-door argument about the Passat and Behija Zukic today and this witness was not present to know whether or not Milan Lukic was in town for any of the enumerated counts in the indictment at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: When the witness comes make that argument --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- we'll consider it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But here is what I'd like to prove to you, Your Honour, is I've made a copy, I have five copies of my binder for this Witness 63 and, see, all I've been able to do with the time-frame this Court has given me is I read it once all the way through, six statements, six statements for the single witness over the course of 15 years. And then we try and highlight the next time and then outline in the margins the third time and then do an outline of which I can -- I'm dissatisfied with myself so if you're dissatisfied with me, then it's all on the table. I'm on the table. So you can understand what it takes to do a witness of this horrible thing. This woman was a victim. I have no doubt in my mind and I have to make her cry to prove a point? I have to put it to the witness? The fact of the matter is is I did misspeak because you're right. In the -- but in the statement to the ICTY, that witness said Milan Lukic held a head. In a statement to -- in anticipation of the Boban Simsic trial she said Milan Lukic head a held and in the statement of the Boban Simsic trial he held a head had. Yet in fact in three opposite statements he didn't, an unknown Serbian, and so I misspeak because I don't have an assistant scrolling through the testimony every time. You allow them to double team me in objections. They split a witness, every day I come they take a new witness. If I had a law firm with eight lawyers I'd be doing gang busters with this case. So I'd like to tell the Court right now because the states been asking me for updates for my defence and what it is and you tell me today I've got to have a full list of witnesses on October 17th and I'm telling you I can't under any set of circumstances with a competent lawyer's ability unless you just believe we're here wasting our time. That's the only way I can do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, let me consider what you have --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But, no, I need to show you something, one more thing, because it's important that you see what's happened to our thing. Can we pull up our photo, please. I'd like to pull up 1D10-1620 for the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is this --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: It's demonstrative aid, Your Honour, so you can see what I'm telling you is true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We don't wish to see it. I think we can determine this matter without looking at your exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, because I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I want to tell the position --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] in relation to co-counsel? Why don't you have a co-counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, see, Your Honour, despite the fact that all 21 counts are against us and we have to answer every count every day, 92 ter gives them 15 minutes and then I have two hours of which to annoy this Court with my questions and the fact of the matter is, Your Honour, is they assess us as a level 1, we're a level 1 case, so I'm supposed to do a 300-victim mass murder case with multiple rapes for a level 1, and because the rules in this somewhere way back when people were probably abusing the process came up and decided that these Rules are what set the guidelines for case preparation regardless of when a lawyer's dropped into the process and said you better be ready or else, and I took that very seriously --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I just wanted to make an inquiry into relation to Sredoje Lukic. Mr. Cepic is the counsel, and Mr. Dieckmann is co-counsel. So in that case I don't understand why Mr. Milan Lukic's case is more voluminous and doesn't have a co-counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, what it is is this: It's the practical application of some backwards rules that don't apply to facts of an individual case. It's an attempt by the registry to cookie cutter this process despite the fact that in and of itself the execution of that violates the processes of due process. The fact the matter is, Your Honour, is that I cannot speak publicly over the registry's issues because some of those issues do involve my client's interactions with previous counsel and the problems that manifested from that. Also the problems involved with my previous lead counsel who deferred to me and then left me holding the bag so the fact of the matter is is I have this case and I've done the best I can but I've had to do with it more grunt workers as opposed to lawyers, and so now I'm in a position being forced on this fast track to get this job done, and this case is not a level 1 because what a level 1 allows for is co-counsel, lead counsel, and a single assistant. You've seen Jelena Rasic here. She is my right hand in terms of handling Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. I'm trying to think of a practical way to resolve it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, all of the arguments that you are raising about the lack of co-counsel have been put to the registrar?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: All the way up to the point of where they tell me my best bet is to appeal to the President, and the fact of the matter is, Your Honours, we'll be done by that point and they bait and switched the whole process at that juncture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But you haven't -- you haven't followed --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- the process by appealing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: When do I have time, really, I mean, I want you to be honest, I mean tell me I'm working, I need a bone here, but the fact of the matter is we come to work every day and it's actually up now, 1D10-1620, please 8, 8, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't want to look at it now. I'm listening to your argument which I consider to be a substantial argument that affects the fairness of the trial. That's why I'm attending to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, and so here's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: So here is the process, Your Honour, is when I left this case I asked this Court, the Tribunal and everyone else. I gave my calendars. I had to go work on this electronically back home while Marie and a couple law students put this case together on paper. We come back here and we start witnesses. That's the way it works and then they don't give enough funding because I have an investigator, a translator and my legal assistant and they want me to hire a co-counsel, but here's what they tell you to do, see if they'll take less money, so I got to talk to people that live in this community and pay their rent out of this budget and I got to start jockeying around. Why? Because the registry doesn't want to account what a real case takes to work it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Alarid, this is what we'll do. We'll take the matter under consideration. The Trial Chamber has to be very careful. Of course when an issue of the fairness of the trial is involved, the Trial Chamber does have jurisdiction, but as you yourself have pointed out, the normal route for challenging a decision of the registrar is to go to the -- to the President. But we are going to look at the matter, and we'll tell you what decision we have come to. In the meantime, I should bring it to your attention that we have responded in some way to the pressure which you obviously are under by granting the reduction from five days to four days. So we haven't been insensitive to your position, and I'd like you to note that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And I did, Your Honour, and I did, but I'll tell you what hurt my feelings because actually that did make me feel good because I did feel respected, but then you took it away at the break. And so it kind of gave me the feeling like, okay, when am I supposed to do this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Took what away?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: The time. The time, Judge. It's all about time. When you did the two weeks and then the one week off and then start and you tell me I got to have a full witness list on the 17th. I mean, when are we supposed to be ready for a Defence case. And, Your Honour, I'd like to think that in any case where a rape victim comes up and says a couple different things in each statement, that is a case. You know, we have the young gentleman that said his friend was killed, pot shot in the water. That disgusts me. Jeez. Who is going to throw a boy over the railing and take a pot shot in the water. But his dad comes on and says he put his twin on the bus before it ever happened even though the one witness said the twin watched him leave in that red Passat that we are also famously chasing. The fact is I believe we have a case here. And how am I supposed to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: How am I supposed to chase down leads? I haven't been to Bosnia yet, Your Honour. I was hoping you have granted the thing so I can go too, the site visit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, as I said, we will take what you have said under consideration, and tomorrow we'll give -- express our views on it, but of course the Chamber has its own jurisdiction to consider in this matter. I mean, this is an institution where various bodies have various institutions, and we'll have to take that into consideration as well. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just briefly. And of course the Prosecution's concerned with the fairness of proceedings as well. If I'm not mistaken, Mr. Ivetic who has arrived here last week is -- has acted ably as a co-counsel in other cases, if I'm not mistaken, so perhaps when the Chamber's considering a possible options, it might want to explore Mr. Alarid and Mr. Ivetic if that were a possibility since he is already working on the case in some capacity and he has appeared before this Tribunal as co-counsel, it might be one sensible solution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we will, bearing in mind of course it is not the Chamber who actually --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: To be honest, Your Honour, that's what I was doing and that was the whole point and I've already submitted the paperwork to the appoint Mr. Ivetic is a legal assistant so he can kind of wade in, you know, get on the treadmill so you're not -- and catch up to speed and I can't get a response on that because I think what they're afraid of is exactly the situation which is becoming clear, which is at the point I hire him as a legal assistant, we're maxed out on the budget, so the fact is is I have to fire people today despite the fact that Mr. Ivetic has to come up to speed and it's not going to come up in a week. It's going to be longer than that to come up to speed. That's the ultimate quandary, the rock and the hard place that we're fighting with here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. As I said, we will consider the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And there is one important issue that I can't forget to say and it kind of goes to the stress of things is Jelena Rasic, that young lady that you've seen here during trial, she's doing legwork investigation right now in Bosnia and she's being threatened. She's getting text messages that are threatening her life right now. So there's this point of time where I got to bring her back here to sign an affidavit to say how dangerous this process is to defend Milan Lukic and try and go get some county court type records and those kind of things. It's really difficult to get things done. And -- and -- you know, but I'm at a point where I have no choice but to send a young girl into the field to do what I think is dangerous work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, that's -- that's another matter. I don't say it is insignificant, but as I indicated, we'll consider the matter and to the extent that we can we'll let you know what our position is tomorrow. Let the witness be called. Thank you very much. I wanted to say, Mr. Alarid, that I did say that you were developing this reputation for misstating the evidence, and that was just a factual statement. I never intended to suggest that it was being done maliciously or with any intent.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, I would just state that that is the level of my preparedness and I don't like it because I actually think you deserve a crisper, cleaner more focussed cross-examination for each and every witness that gets the point and does it. But of course, these are beautiful people that come in front of us, and they don't want to answer my questions because they know who I represent, and so we go around the pole some -- way too many times and I don't want to hurt them. That is a horrible position to be put in because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You must have done very well before a jury, Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, I like to talk to people because I think, you know what, we all take the robes off and are just people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Alarid. Thank you very much. The witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. At this time the Prosecution calls VG-82.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: VG-82, yes. We have spent about 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit, and you may begin, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. At this time the Prosecution would request the court usher to hand the witness a pseudonym sheet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: VG-82, you've been granted certain protective measures by the Trial Chamber including the use of a pseudonym. Directing your attention to the sheet in front of you, does your name appear on that sheet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: Yes, it is my name on the paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Does your date of birth also appear on that sheet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you please sign that sheet?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At this time the Prosecution would tender that sheet into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the pseudonym sheet will become P115 under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: VG-82, did you provide a statement to ICTY investigators on the 31st of October, 1997, and also on the 26th of January, 2001?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to review that statement in the Bosnian language before coming to court here today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If you were asked today the same questions as you were asked when you provided that statement, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is the statement that you provided true and accurate to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At this time the Prosecution offers 65 ter number 185 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is admitted as Exhibit P116 under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: VG-82, in your statement you refer to Milan Lukic as your pupil. When was Milan Lukic your student?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: It could have been in the school year of 1982, '83.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Where was Milan Lukic a student of yours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: In the secondary school centre in Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What was your position at the secondary school centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: I was a teacher.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What are the ages of the students who attend the secondary school centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: Their years of birth would have been from 1974 to 1978 -- sorry, '64 to '68.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You're referring to the birth years of 1964 through 1968. Are there particular years in which you were a professor at the secondary school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: I worked there in the school year 1981, '82, and school year 1982, '83.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And would these birth years been the ages of the students who attended the school during the years in which you were employed there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What grade and class did you instruct Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: He was in year two of the secondary school when I taught him. He was the 29 class, and that was for cooks and waiters, that is, for the catering industry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Was Milan Lukic a part of a programme that related to this education?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: Yes. He was in this course and I remember well he was in the front row, the last bench in the front row, together with Izet Tabakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: How long did students attend the secondary school? Precisely how many years did the students go to the school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: The secondary school course is three to four years depending on whether they are getting a general education or training for a particular vocation. Milan Lukic's course was three years. Engineering courses took four years, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: VG-82, I'd like you to take a look around the courtroom here today. Could you please indicate whether or not you recognise anyone in the courtroom aside from myself and Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And standard objection to the form of identification, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it's noted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: VG-82, are you able to see everyone in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: I can see everyone, and I recognise two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. What are the names of the individuals that you recognise in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: To my left in the third row, the second person from the wall is Milan Lukic. Next to him, that is the third person in the last row, is Sredoje Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You're referring to the second and third person in the last row. Are you counting from your left or your right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: From my left. On my left-hand side counting from the left to the right they are the second and the third person.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: May the record reflect the in-court identifications of Milan Lukic as the second person from the left and Sredoje Lukic as the third person from the left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Mr. VG-82, my name is Jason Alarid and I'm the lawyer for Milan Lukic. Can we ask you a few questions, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, you did review your statement of 1994, as well as your statement to the ICTY in 2001 and 1997; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, the one thing I didn't understand is how could a statement be both from 1997 and 2001 but written in one statement. Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: From what I know, there are two separate statements. One was given on the subject of Behija Zukic, and the second statement was given about me and the execution I survived. So in total, there should be two statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And that's two statements to the ICTY; correct? Which would make three statements total. And the reason I say that is because what I have in my folder that's been disclosed by the Prosecution is a 1994 statement to the MUP in Gorazde, and then I have a statement to the ICTY that says that there were interviews in the 31st of October, 1997, and the 26th of January, 2001, a four-year differential. Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: Maybe we did not understand each other really. I said I gave two statements, one about Behija Zukic and another concerning me personally. I gave one statement in Gorazde, that's true, and the second statement I gave subsequently to the investigator. So one statement was made in Gorazde, and there's another one given to the investigator. There are two different subjects in two different statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so was there an actual statement produced in 1997 that you reviewed and signed, whether it was about yourself or Behija Zukic? Did you review and sign anything in 1997?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: I had the opportunity to review each of the statements I've given.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Do you remember giving a statement in 1997 to an investigator from the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is objection just right now. I believe the question is a little unclear. There's only two statements that the ICTY has disclosed. There's only two statements that exist. One of the statements, the ICTY statement, was -- this witness was interviewed in 1997, then I believe the witness signed the statement in 2001. I believe Mr. Alarid would like to direct the witness's attention relating to that. This witness has clearly indicated at this time there's only two statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: That sort of did clarify things, Your Honour, from Mr. Weber, although I'd kind of like it to come from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Do you remember -- so you were interviewed in 1997? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: I think it was in 1997 when I gave that statement in Gorazde, and later, in 2001, if I'm not mistaken, I gave another statement to the investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And in 2001 -- but I mean -- actually, back that up. In 1997 was any piece of paper prepared as a result of that first interview to the ICTY investigator for you to review?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: Maybe you should clarify, because I haven't quite understood what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, I have a statement that says that there were two interviews, in 1997 and 2001. My query is did anyone prepare a preliminary statement in 1997 for you to review and possibly sign?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: I know that I signed a statement, and I believe it was in 2001, the statement that I gave to the investigators. So that's the 2001 statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so my next question is though if you didn't sign anything in 1997, was at least something prepared for you that memorialised the investigation that you reviewed for accuracy even if you didn't sign it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: You see, from the events in Visegrad, so even in those times of war when some people thought it was impossible to document certain things, we had already started, actually, putting the facts on paper, even before the war was over. And after the Dayton Accords, it became much easier, but even during the war we had been trying to document the events and facts and everything that happened in Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, isn't it true that from a time period standpoint, your statements involving Milan Lukic or your knowledge of Milan Lukic precede the 1st of June, 1992, don't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: As for my knowledge of Milan Lukic the statement was about the war and what happened during the war. I provided a statement on what happened during the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Mr. -- I'm not sure I understand the question. Is the question whether he gave statements --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Regarding --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- Milan Lukic before the 1st of June 1992 --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Then it was a very bad question if that's where it is. I'll try and clarify it then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: No, sir, what I'm actually asking you is isn't it true in your statement you testified about what you believed happened between Behija Zukic, the red Passat, and Milan Lukic's involvement in that? Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: It's not what I believed, it's what I saw. I eyewitnessed that, and I also heard things about it, both. It's about what happened in 1991 and 1992 over there during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But would it be fair to say that as your statement relates to Milan Lukic, your involvement or what you saw all occurred before the 1st of June, 1992? Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: What happened with Behija Zukic was in May 1992. My own case happened in June, the 11th of June 1992. So we're talking about May and June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what happened to you in June of 1992 is when you were taken away and arrested by some Serbians whom you did not know and were almost executed. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: So whatever you knew about Milan Lukic or observed about Milan Lukic preceded the 1st of June and is related to the death of Behija Zukic. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: That's true. Prior to the 1st of June Behija Zukic's death occurred. It was back in May. That, however, does not mean that Milan Lukic did not continue his activities over the following months, although that doesn't necessarily apply to my own case in June.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, and it also doesn't apply to what you would be able to observe and testify under oath about. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: Can you please clarify that for me?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Meaning you can't testify from personal knowledge of any witnessing of Milan Lukic or doing anything after what you saw surrounding Behija Zukic occurred.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: I was still following everything that was happening even after what occurred to Behija Zukic, because I was still in the Visegrad municipal area. I remained in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so your interest after that was more curiosity and following the news as opposed to actually witnessing any part of what Milan Lukic may or may not have done after the end of May 1992. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: After the end of May 1992 and June. Up until the 11th of June, 1992 I was an eyewitness in Visegrad because I was in Visegrad itself, in the centre of Visegrad. After the 11th of June, I could no longer follow any developments or indeed what Milan Lukic was doing simply because the town by this point in time had been cleansed already.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But you were -- but the last time that you believe you saw Milan Lukic was before the end of June 1992. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: Well, yes. The 11th of June is the time up until which I was able to see him around town but not after that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so are you testifying today that you saw him around town between of 1st of June, let's say, and the 11th of June?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And have you testified to this before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And where did you see him specifically on the 1st of June, let's say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: Let me tell you. It has been 17 years since. You're asking me about the 1st of June specifically. Who on earth could possibly remember such a thing? But he was seen around town every day with this Passat, the car, cherry red, and sometimes he would walk around town with no car, but he was also known for walking around Visegrad barefoot with no shoes on so that no one could hear him as he approached certain homes and certain facilities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, you say that he was seen around town every day with this Passat. Did you actually see him? Were you one of those persons who saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was able to see him around town, yes. Sometimes during the day we would need to go out and get some bread or some supplies in the centre. Movement, however, was quite restricted simply because movement was not always possible. There were always situations in which somebody would say, "Here comes Lukic. Here comes the Passat." And that was a sign for anyone who happened to be around to try to get off the street as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And do you realise that you didn't state any of that in your 1997/2000 report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Statement you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is that what you call a report or is it a statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The statement, yes. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Isn't it true, sir, that in your statement of 1997 or 2001 you did not mention seeing Milan Lukic in a Passat or barefoot or walking around between the day Behija Zukic's body was taken from her house and June 11th when you left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, in my statement the only reference to Milan Lukic is in connection with the Behija Zukic situation. This is not something that I mentioned in my statement. The only thing I mention in my statement is what happened to Behija Zukic, which is also what I saw and also what I heard from other people over the phone or when talking to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I want to know what you saw, when you were, where you were, when you saw him, was a barefoot, was he driving or was he walking, what you saw?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Those are a series of compound questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ask them singly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Let's just say after May 31st, [Realtime transcript read in error "July 1st"] 1992, where was the first place you saw Milan Lukic and where?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first place I saw Milan Lukic after the 1st of July was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm allowing that question. I don't consider it sufficiently compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just want to correct the transcript, actually. It says July 1st. I believe counsel intended June 1st.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I just wanted to --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Actually, I meant May 31st.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. I was just correcting the transcript, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And, sir, could you repeat yourself? The transcript did not pick up the translation. After May 31st, 1992, where was the first place you saw Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: The first place I saw Milan Lukic was a cafe along a street in Visegrad close to a building that was known as number 8. That's what we called the building. It was a very famous building. It had eight floors. There was this cafe behind that building and Milan used to go there a lot. I'm not sure if he actually owned the cafe, but it's just behind the building that we refer to as number 8. This is a street that takes you from the centre of town to Prelovo and his native area of Rujiste.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Was he in the cafe?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Where were you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: After the murder of Behija Zukic I and other people who lived in that neighbourhood moved closer to the town itself because they had told us that the is Serb police did not have sufficient manpower to make sure everybody was safe and there were killings occurring. They told us that we should move closer to the town itself and they would thus be better able to better establish some effective control over what was going on. This is when I arrived in the building that we refer to as number 8, because that's where my son-in-law lived, and he put us up. That means me, my wife, and my child.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, just a few days earlier you had hidden in an attic and, I believe, saw the body of Behija Zukic through a hole you had made in the roof tiles. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And -- but before that night you didn't know she had died until someone told you because you were again hiding under a bridge avoiding capture. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: You see, we were hiding under the bridge. We started hiding the moment Behija Zukic informed us that her husband, Dzemo Zukic, her son Faruk Zukic, Fehim Tabakovic and his two sons, Izet Tabakovic and Ferid Tabakovic, and Fahrudin Cocalic had been taken away on her lorry. There was this pick-up truck, a TAM truck that Behija Zukic owned, and these people were put onto that truck and taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, what I'd asked you was is you were hiding under the bridge the night of. Isn't that true? I know you want to say more, but I'd like to get you home. So you'd just been hided under a bridge; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: That night and after what had happened I was under the bridge that had been destroyed. When the hydroelectric plant started operating the bridge was blown up and that's where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And I'm assuming that you had to make it to your -- is it your brother-in-law's home? Is that where you stayed after that? Sorry?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: I was at Dusce because the hydroelectric power plant was not functioning properly anymore and the water wreaked a lot of destruction so I was staying in my brother Hilmo's place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And that's in building number 8; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: No. Just to make sure we're perfectly clear about this. After all of this happened, after the murder of Behija Zukic, I moved to the number 8 to stay with my son-in-law. And what happened earlier on, what happened in connection with Behija Zukic, during that time I was staying with my brother in the neighbourhood in which I lived. That was after Behija Zukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. And so when you're in -- when you're in building number 8 you're having to hide; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And I'm assume you're keeping the windows shuttered and the curtains closed; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: Well, yes. It was like that for the most part. It's just that the windows weren't facing the cafe but, rather, the other way, the Elektrodistribucija company, which was another street, the street opposite, so that's the way the windows were facing, but anyway, we weren't really able to look out. We had to lie underneath our beds and sofas, for example, when someone came knocking at our door.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so how were you able to see this Milan Lukic at the cafe from number 8 and can you tell me what day of the 11 days you were there that you were able to see him at the cafe?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: I think I was quite clear when I said that. I could see him when I left the number 8 and I told you a while ago that we would sometimes go out to get our supplies such as bread and milk, because we had left our own homes, and I had to get some food. I couldn't get by without food, and I was certainly in no position to use anyone else's food. We would go out and get supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But isn't it true at this time Visegrad was crawling with Serbian extremists?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: Yes, but I told you how it was, roughly speaking. One would leave and go out as quickly as possible but nip over to a shop or grocery to get some milk or other supplies, and as quickly as you could you would just walk back. At a later stage even that no longer worked, so we would just send our wives for them to go and get supplies just in order to make sure that no men were out in the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what day between June 1st and June 11th did you see Milan Lukic at the cafe?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: It might have been the first days of June, the 1st or the 2nd, perhaps, but it's difficult to be very specific because he spent a lot of time in that cafe.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Was he there every day and you saw him there every day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: The days that I left the house, whenever I was actually out to get some supplies. If I never left the house, as the case was on certain days, I wasn't able to see him, was I?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, sir, you've been brought here to rebut an alibi testimony it, so it's very important that you're able to pinpoint with certainty of date the date you saw him.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: As I said, it's very difficult now, 17 years later. You're asking me about the exact date. The next thing I know you'll be asking me about the hour of the day, but it has been a long time. However, up until the 11th of June, the beginning of the Bajram holiday, I was trying to leave, to get out. Whenever I thought it was safe to get out of the house, I would go and get some basic supplies. Those were the basic necessities. That's why I would go out of the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so you're saying despite needing to hide in attics and under a bridge, you could walk out in broad daylight and go shopping?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: I told you we would just nip out in a manner of speaking and try to keep it as quick and as short as possible, and there were shops nearby. The neighbourhood is called Mezalin. There were shops nearby. You could just go in and out in no time at all, get your supplies and be gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: How many times did you go out versus sending your wives?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: Well, let's say once a day. I was in no position to risk more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: So you're saying you went outside every day between June 1st and June 11th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: During the daylight?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: Yes. Daytime, of course --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Just to shop for the --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: -- because of the business hours of the shops. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, if men are being taken away never to be seen again don't you think it would be more prudent to gather enough supplies to last for a while?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, things had not yet begun to happen in the same intense way that they started happening later on. By this time only two murders had occurred, no more than two. The first involved the Smajic family, the wife and the husband, Medo Smajic and his wife. That was the first murder. And then there was Behija Zukic, which was the next murder. Maybe at this time people were not yet fully aware of how the whole thing would end and what it would eventually lead to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Sir, before this date the Uzice Corps had already come to town, hadn't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: Before when?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Before the death of Behija Zukic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. The Uzice Corps came in on the 14th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And the Uzice Corps, while they were in town many crimes were committed against Muslims, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: Well, they were more like putting in their measuring rod and then checking, but the murders really started occurring in any serious way once the Uzice Corps had withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And the Uzice Corps disarmed the Muslim people, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. I don't think what there was to take away in terms of disarming and who in Visegrad could be disarmed in terms of owning weapons. When the hydroelectric power plant was abandoned, all the Muslims left Visegrad. When they were returning, no one was allowed to carry any weapons while returning. Therefore, there was no one and nothing to disarm.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And during the Uzice Corps Muslim men disappeared, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: Well, I told you it was mostly about people being taken away and people being checked. The Uzice Corps was headquartered at Bikavac. Mostly there were interviews that were being conducted during the presence of the Uzice Corps in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Sir, in your statement of 1997 and 2001, you indicated that the White Eagles participated in the attack on Dobrun on the 6th of April, 1992. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: Yes, that's true, the 6th of April, 1992. The White Eagles attacked the local commune of Dobrun. This local commune straddles the border with Serbia. I'm talking about Serbia the country. On the 6th of April, the White Eagles attacked Dobrun. There are documents showing that that were seized, those documents, the White Eagles documents, with all their first names, last names, personal detail, as well as their rules of conduct. But they had tags on them that said Eagles, and then also a flag was seized as well as some other material.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you heard about the entire population, the Muslim population, as many as they could gather were taken to the soccer stadium, the football stadium in Visegrad and addressed by Colonel Jovanovic. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: Yes. I heard that people had been taken to the stadium. Probably the objective was to take them away, cleansing. The aim was to use buses to ferry them across to other countries and other areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And isn't it true that in that stadium Colonel Jovanovic claimed he controlled the White Eagles? Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: I wasn't at the stadium myself. Did I hear this, did I not hear this, frankly I don't remember. Nevertheless, as long as the Uzice Corps was still around, the situation was more or less bearable. Once it left, everything changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Or quite possibly it was a calculated attempt at disarming the Muslim people, then luring them back to their homes to be victimised and unarmed by a well-organised police action.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: Let me tell you this: All of the people who returned, returned unarmed. There was no resistance at all on their part. That was out of the question. You could say the aim of the whole thing was to bring people back into town, and then we know what happened later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, let's talk about how you know Milan Lukic. You remember him specifically being in your class?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: Yes, I do, specifically. And I told you what his class was, the number, the department, and what the vocational speciality was that they were studying. If required, I can provide further explanations as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, but isn't it true that in your statement you didn't necessarily recognise Milan Lukic and it was a Mr. Tabakovic who told you or reminded you that he was somehow in your class?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: You see, when Milan Lukic came from Obrenovac, Serbia, to Visegrad his behaviour drew a lot of attention from many of us. As an individual, as a human being, what he did drew some interest. We actually tried to find out more about him because of that. This is just a single source. Izet Tabakovic who was his classmate and Tesalic [phoen], they were classmates. But this is just a single source that sort of filled in whatever information I had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, we're going to take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Mr. Tabakovic is the one that you said was a schoolmate or classmate with Milan Lukic? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And which year was he a classmate with him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: I think it was the school year 1982, '83. And they were in the second year of secondary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And the -- but the reality is you couldn't remember him. You needed this other young man to tell -- or remind you, rather, that he was in your class. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: That young man is just one of the sources I told you a moment ago. Izet Tabakovic and Fahrudin Cocalic were his classmates. And there is another source that I checked and indeed was convinced that it was a former student of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What was the other source, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: One is my own inquiries that I made into him, because for a while he was absent from Visegrad, having continued his studies in Belgrade before coming back to our area. So for a while I wasn't seeing him, and then I tried to gather more information to put the whole picture together, which I did, and the other source are those two young men.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Where did you make those inquiries?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: In town, in contacts with people of both Bosniak and Serb ethnicity. The two communities were still communicating.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: How about school records?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: School records exist. There are yearbooks that are kept in the school and archived for a number of years, and they can be checked.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so you're positive that this Milan Lukic in his second year of secondary school was in your class, personally taught by you. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: You're certain of this to a hundred per cent. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: I'm quite certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you believe school records and yearbooks will verify this. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: Yes, because these yearbooks, books kept for every class, exist. They are archived.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And if I were to tell you that this Milan Lukic was in fact not your student and attended a different curriculum, would that change your testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: I'll tell you, I'm convinced that he was in that particular course at school, and I taught all classes from year 1 to year 4 of that school, and there were a total of 11 different courses given -- giving different vocational training leading to different professions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: How about metallurgy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: There was a course in metallurgy, and I taught that course too. Those were locksmiths, metal grinders, lathe operators, metallurgical technicians. All these were different vocations at school and I taught them as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How many students did you teach in all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That secondary school centre had around 1.500 students, and it worked in two shifts. So there is a likelihood that I taught around half of that total, around 700 to 800 students following different courses in different years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Now, the class in which you say Milan was, how many students would it have had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the classes were up to 30 students. Up to 30 students were in one classroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is there anything specific about Milan Lukic that you remember as a student?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that period he didn't stand out. He was young. He was around 17. At that time he didn't stand out because he didn't know himself at the time what would happen in ten years. If he had known, maybe his conduct would have been different even then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But in fact in your statement of 1997, 2001, you stated that: "He was not a noticeable pupil and, frankly, I don't really remember him clearly from that time." Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: That's what I said a moment ago. He wasn't particularly remarkable at the time. However, after the events that followed ten years later, his behaviour changed. He couldn't have told himself who he would become ten years later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Because the Milan Lukic that you believe went to school and you taught was not an aggressive student or did not cause fights or anything? Is that the fact?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, when you -- after the death of Behija Zukic, you heard that members of your community went to complain to the commander in chief, Risto Perisic. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And isn't it true that Risto Perisic was the chief of police as well as a high ranking member of the Crisis Stab and the SDS party?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: Risto Perisic was my former classmate -- sorry, my former work colleague. We used to work together in the secondary school centre. He taught the Serbian language. When the war broke out, when the military operation started, Risto Perisic became chief of MUP. So he was the chief of MUP, a member of the SDS, and a member of the Crisis Staff. So he was in the inner circle of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And being in the inner circle of the SDS, the SDS held absolute control over the police in Visegrad after the break-up. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: Yes. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And isn't it true that Dragan Tomic was the commander of the police under Perisic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And isn't it true that many Muslims were arrested by the police under the control of Risto Perisic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And many of those Muslims were never seen or heard from again. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, you heard that Milan Lukic lived in Obrenovac. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: Yes. After completing two years of secondary school he continued his schooling at the police school in Belgrade. You may wonder how come there were so many Lukices in the police and I'll tell you. They have a relative in Belgrade, a certain Lukic, who was the secretary of the Ministry of the Interior. In other words, the minister. And through that Lukic many Lukices were admitted into active police service after -- after completing training.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, you have used up 55 minutes, and I'll allow you another ten.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: So you're -- so you're not saying that this Milan Lukic finished as a cook; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: When he was finishing his second year, since there were not enough trained active policemen a public competition was announced with the following terms: After two years of no matter what kind of secondary training, one could continue in a police training course to become an active duty policeman. And following that line, Milan Lukic, as an ethnic Serb, and Samir Dedic, an ethnic Bosnian, continued their schooling in a police school, because Samir Dedic's father was also a policeman, Hasim [as interpreted] Dedic. The two continued their schooling, reorienting from their original secondary course to police training.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so do I -- so does it stand to reason that the information that you got regarding this Milan Lukic moving to Obrenovac and continuing in the police academy was through Samir Dedic's father? That's where you did your research. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, are we still in private session? Yes. May the court assistant assist me in taking a pseudonym sheet to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And, sir, what's being handed to you is a pseudonym sheet, and just like yourself, other witnesses have been granted protective measures, and I'm going to ask you, do you know who VG-115 is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: How many people were in building 8 when you were staying there before you departed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: In which building?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Where you were hiding before you left June 11th.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: In number 8 there were several Bosniak families. There was the family of Teufo Tankovic. That's him and his wife Savala.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I don't mean to cut you off, but what I was concerned about was did at any time you know this person is staying in building 8? Just a query. Even if you didn't know them personally, did you know who she was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-82
utterances.text: I neither heard nor saw them.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, I was perplexed by the statement you made in your remarks concerning the giving of a decision by the Trial Chamber before you had had a chance to respond. I've had it investigated, and this is what happened: The Trial Chamber gave a decision only in relation to VG-42. We have not given a decision in relation to the other witnesses mentioned in the Prosecution's motion. And you did reply in relation to VG-42.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So I'd like to have that clear on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: 42 and 65 were separated, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: We separated those, considering you were clearly dealing with the issues of those two separate from the ones that are actually due today, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, so I just wanted to have it clarified that the Trial Chamber did not give a decision in relation to any witness in respect of whom you have not yet responded.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. I just have a final matter with regard to this witness. I think considering the fact that he was tendered only under the alibi exception following the final 65 ter list and witness list, the witness was not able to give any relevant testimony against the alibi testimony. He was not able to give any specific dates for the relevant counts in June, and specifically he was best able to comment both in his statement, as well as today as to times before the relevant conduct is in issue. If all he was brought in to was to do alibi, I would move that his testimony be stricken. If the Court considers it otherwise, then we would like his MUP statement introduced into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, have you heard that submission? Mr. Weber, the submission is that the witness whom we just heard did not give evidence to rebut the alibi. The witness gave evidence on other matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
