utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd refer the Chamber's attention to the decision that was rendered on the 29th of August, 2008, when this Chamber allowed this witness -- specifically paragraphs 28 and 29. This witness was allowed by the Chamber to present evidence relating to three specific Defence alibi witnesses MLD 5, MLD 6 and MLD 8. It fell within the scope of rebuttal evidence because it rebuts factual assertions that were offered by these Defence witnesses. Believe this witness's testimony should be weighed in context of those witnesses that will appear before the Chamber. The Chamber found that this evidence of this witness is relevant to rebut Defence alibi evidence, not just specifically an alibi. So it -- the Chamber deemed this witness appropriate and relevant to rebut Defence alibi evidence specifically coming from three witnesses, as indicated by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, I know the Chamber allowed it, but that's not the point. The point is whether the evidence that we actually heard is properly classifiable as alibi rebuttal evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the evidence that the Prosecution indicated in its motion which the Chamber allow was admitted today pursuant to 92 ter. The Prosecution because of the five-minute time limit that was allotted by the Chamber to not lead this evidence, we do not have any objection to counsel's request to admit also the 1994 statement and this was the evidence that this witness was intended to give before the Chamber and the evidence that the witness did provide today in the form of 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ultimately -- Mr. Alarid, ultimately these are all matters that the Trial Chamber as the trier of fact will have to determine, to determine what weight to attach to the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, I mean on one hand, Your Honour, I would agree had they listed this witness in their case in chief. I think from that perspective it -- what can I say? But from the perspective of specifically stating that this witness has information that rebuts an alibi, and an alibi is "I was not here, I was somewhere else." This guy did not say, "No, Milan was here instead of somewhere else." Given that fact, during the 11 days he may have seen him at a cafe, that still doesn't necessarily negate alibi. And I understand where they're going is because one of the submissions that my predecessor put in his initial alibi statement way back in January was that Milan says he wasn't always in the Passat, and therefore I think this is still chasing that cherry red Passat, but it doesn't necessarily go to the meat and bones of what an alibi is, which is, "I wasn't there when they say I was," and if he was another witness who said, "Oh, I saw him on June 7th," I would understand if he was another witness who said that, but he didn't say that. So that's why I make my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The three witnesses which were submitted by Defence counsel who is before the now are MLD 5, MLD 6 and MLD 8. All three of these witnesses indicate that others besides Milan Lukic drove the red Passat and also call into question about whether or not he killed Behija Zukic. These -- then during this case the very first witness, actually, counsel made quite an issue and has continued to make an issue over the ownership and possession of this red Passat. This witness was called for a specific purpose relating to rebuttal evidence of facts that contradict the facts which may or may not be offered by the three Defence witnesses MLD 5, MLD 6, or MLD 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We heard the submissions made by Mr. Alarid, and we'll take them into consideration. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I said to the Court that I would investigate the matter of disclosure last Friday and I do have some additional information for the Chamber. With respect to Ewa Tabeau, 955 pages in total were provided Defence counsel. Nearly half of that, 466 pages, are her reports from completely unrelated cases. They were provided as a courtesy upon the request of the Defence and not because they were disclosable. And these are cases having to do with the events in Srebrenica in 1995, the Prlic case, cases arising out of the Krajina. So they are cases that clearly have no bearing on this case but again were provided at the request of the Defence counsel. Also disclosed were 200 pages of her report for the Vasiljevic case. That was previously disclosed, Your Honour. All that was disclosed Friday was an ERNed copy because that's the copy that would be used in court with her if she was referring to her report. So that's 200 pages that had been previously disclosed. Also disclosed were 175 pages of her report for the Milosevic case, and this was the B/C/S translation of that report. The English version of the Milosevic report was disclosed in March of 2007. So in summary, Your Honour, out of the 955 pages referred to, 840 of those pages were either provided as a courtesy to Defence upon their request or were previously disclosed documents. With respect to Dr. John Clark, our IT people conducted a search of records having John Clark's name and identified several thousands of documents. Approximately 900 of these documents arise out of forensic examinations that he was involved with in some capacity arising out of Slap, and the Chamber has already heard of Slap as the communal grave site where many of the victims of what happened in Visegrad were buried. Nine hundred and four documents were disclosed. Out of these 904 pages, approximately 100 pages are text and 800 pages are diagrams of bodies showing the location where the body was recovered and/or diagrams of the bodies showing where injuries were sustained. These documents represent the records of 131 forensic examinations, not all personally performed by Clark. Out of these 131, only 3 have direct relevance to this case, and these have been identified to Defence counsel. These are approximately 9 pages of text. As a final note, Your Honour, as the Court is well aware, these cases do generate a lot of -- a large number of documents, and it's for that reason that I had asked my staff to disclose what was properly disclosable under Rule 66 and Rule 68 and then make Defence counsel aware of any other documents that they may also be interested in and as a courtesy to them provide them if they so wished, and that is why so many documents were provided on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. Who is your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution's next witness is Ms. Ewa Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. Just a minute, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Marcus. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, by your leave I just wish to reply to Mr. Groome's statement. If the material is not relevant, why has it been disclosed to us? We had 1.334 pages to work with Saturday morning. I was really in no position to judge which of them were relevant to our case and which were not. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: As a courtesy, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the history of it is when the staff identified these documents to me, I drafted a letter which was sent to Defence counsel at the end of last week notifying them of this body of material and offering them, if they wanted to, to view it. The response was they did want this material and it was provided, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So apparently you did request it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. There has been some confusion, it seems. We were invited by Mr. Cole from the OTP by e-mail to inspect all the material quite unrelated to this material that was not meant to be disclosed. That was the invitation we received from Mr. Cole. And this disclosure was on an entirely different basis. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Either way, Your Honour, the offering of Mr. Groome was at the end of Friday, and then we get into the position of getting more disclosures over weekend, and the offer to or the request to see the census materials as well as the voter registration materials we made today and our initial response was simply that under Rule 70 they could not other than allowing us to come into the building. I think that's why I filed a motion or an objection to bar the testimony of this witness in advance of the Chamber's session today and I don't want to waive that motion and I feel that we're at a disadvantage to cross-examination today with those matters disclosed at such a late point or at least left outstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Beginning of Friday. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau is readily available. If the Chamber thinks in fairness to both Defence counsel that they should have an additional opportunity or they should have the opportunity to look at this 9.5 million populated database of voter registration, again Ms. Tabeau is here at the beck and call of the Chamber to assist in any way she can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. But we'll certainly proceed with the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: You have been called to testify as an expert in these proceedings. Could you please inform the Court of what your area of expertise is.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I am a demographer. My recent expertise is in the studies of conflict, victims of conflict, the so-called demography of conflict, but from education I am a statistician. I studied statistics and econometrics, obtained my master degree in this area. Later I obtained my Ph.D. in mathematical demography.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: As the Trial Chamber decided in -- on the 23rd of July, 2008, that Dr. Tabeau does qualify as an expert I will -- am not intending to dwell on her professional qualifications. May I just simply request the court officer to pull up ERN that's document ID 0641-6000.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me. May I have some assistant here? I actually pushed some buttons and incorrectly, I believe. I lost my transcript. And if I have something from the e-court it's coming here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've just been informed by the court usher that the document can't be found. May I just have a moment, please, and I'll pull up the hard copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS

utterances.text: We're starting on slide 5, page 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, could you please tell us in general terms what your expert report is about?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: There are two main subjects discussed in this report. The first subject is the changes in the ethnic composition in the period between the outbreak of the conflict and after the conflict ended and related to these numbers of IDPs and refugees from the Visegrad region in Bosnia, and the second subject is an analysis of missing persons from the Visegrad region and Visegrad municipality itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Pages 6. Does this list represent the other cases before this Tribunal in which this methodology has been used?

utterances.text: We are now talking about the first subject I have just mentioned, the analysis of ethnic composition and IDPs and refugees. Yes indeed, this list represents the ICTY cases where this method and this kind of study was presented. Our major study was done for the case of Slobodan Milosevic where the area that we presented was far larger than what we present in this report. It was 47 municipalities in Bosnia then. The results presented in this report originated from this study completed for Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Page 7. Turning to the first issue --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm sorry. I think that the interpreters have a very difficult job because the both witness and my friend Ms. Marcus speak the same language and it is I believe quite difficult to translate everything at times. Thank you very much.

utterances.text: Yes, please observe a pause between question and answer, both witness and counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Turning to the first issue. Could you kindly explain what is the objective of this portion of your analysis?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: The main objective we had in mind was to present -- to obtain, produce reliable statistics on genders in the ethnic composition and on the numbers of internally displaced persons and refugees who originated from the Visegrad region. Sources that would -- could be used for this kind of analysis are limited, practically non-existence when particular conflict periods need to be analysed. So this is a challenge, and we identified the necessary sources in proposed methodology, suitable methodology to work on this objective. Well, the region that we analysed in this particular report, I'm speaking we because the initial report was made with a co-author, with Jakub Bijak. Now I updated myself the Visegrad study. Well, when the area is considered then we -- I have to say the analysis is not only made for the Visegrad municipality but also a number of neighbouring municipalities in the Visegrad region were included in the study, and among the most important were of course Srebrenica, Bratunac, Vlasenica, and other municipalities. I would like at some point to show this region on a map.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes. We can turn to page 8. Does this map represent the geographic scope of your study?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. In the upper right corner there is a square in which the Visegrad region is shown. It is located at the eastern border of Bosnia and Herzegovina with Serbia. So the Visegrad municipality was the central area in our study. And surrounding municipalities included Srebrenica, Bratunac, Vlasenica, Han Pijesak, Sokolac, Rogatica, Cajnice and Rudo. We excluded Gorazde as this municipality was split by the Dayton line and in all split municipalities there were very, very intense population movements across the border of the political entities, so these changes wouldn't be directly comparable with all the changes in all remaining municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: We've placed the PowerPoint presentation on the ELMO so that will also enable Dr. Tabeau to point with her pen as she -- as she speaks. Turning to page 9. Turning back to your sources, Dr. Tabeau, which you referred to before, could you please explain briefly what sources were used for this portion of your study.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: We used two major sources. One was the 1991 population census conducted in March '91 in the entire country in Bosnia-Herzegovina and also for the rest of the former Yugoslavia. And the second source that we used for the post-conflict period were the voters registrations from 1997 and 1998. But as for the starting point of the analysis, the '91 census was the only and major source, and one of a better if not the best source one can imagine to be used in such a study as this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can you -- can you explain, elaborate on why the census is, as you say, one of the best sources which can be used in this study?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: The population census is the complete population survey in every country. So it is conducted only every approximately ten years as it is a huge effort for statistical authority to conduct the census. It covers, as I said, the entire population in a country, and many aspects of the population. In Bosnia the '91 census covered issues related to the population itself, and as a well other issues related to agriculture. We didn't use the agricultural part of the census. We used the data describing the population of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: What was the methodology for dealing with any deficiencies which may exist in a census?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, perhaps first of all I will mention the deficiencies. The major deficiency of the census data is that data was moved from paper copies of the questionnaires used during the census to the computer files by OCRing, optical character recognition techniques were used in order to computerise this material, and during this process errors were made related to -- to the scanning. So these errors can be seen on the first place in the names of the individuals listed in the census. These are spelling mistakes that we had to deal with, and some other mistakes. Recorded categories were far less affected by the misread characters than the names. In order to eliminate the mistakes from the names, names were important for us from the point of view of the methodology used in this study, we applied several techniques. There were at least three major projects in which we corrected the mistakes -- spelling mistakes in the names. First project was basically running a computer programme to detect impossible combinations of letters in the Bosnian language. There were native speakers who defined -- linguists who defined these impossible combination. So these combinations of letters were identified and replaced by the most likely right combinations. The second method was making lists of names as reported and asking native B/C/S speakers to correct the names, to make from their own names misspelled names the right names. And the third method was we applied a household approach in which in every household in the census we tried to identify the right spelling of name -- of the name within this household. Once such a name was identified all other members with misspelled names within the same household received the correct name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, what is the time estimate for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, as Mr. Groome submitted this morning, we were trying to get through this within a reasonable period of time. His estimate was 50 minutes. I will do my very utmost to -- to get through it in that time or very close to that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, we're moving to page 10 of the PowerPoint. Please briefly could you tell us who is included in the voter registers.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: In the voters registers are included eligible voters who registered to vote in the '97 and '98 elections, local elections, in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Those who didn't register are not there and those not eligible to vote, too young, are not included in the registers as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now moving to page 11. Could you briefly describe the methods you used in your study?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, basically we -- our purpose was to produce reliable statistics, and we used original sources, that is the census and the voters registers in order to produce those statistics from individual level data. Ethnicity was, however, an important characteristic of the population, and in order to include ethnicity in our study it was necessary to match the census data with the voters registers. So the basic methodology, the most important part of the methodology is the matching of the two sources. We also applied the matching later to the missing persons list that was matched with the census as well for the same purpose as ethnicity was not reported in the voters and not in the missing persons list.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Page 12. Could you tell us what definition of ethnicity was used?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: The ethnicity definition used was the one from the population census --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I just thought that I heard a leading question, but it's okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please continue, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ethnicity was coming from the census records. This means in the census questionnaire there was a question related to ethnicity. Every respondent had the right to identify himself or herself by giving an answer the person felt was right. It was an open-ended question. All together there were approximately 100 categories reported in the census data. We regrouped these 100 categories with -- into four major groups. We took all those who reported themselves as Serbs to be the Serbs, all those reported as Muslims or Bosniaks as the Muslims, Croats as Croats, and all other ethnicities, including Yugoslavs, in the final last category that we called others. It's important to say that it wasn't so difficult to work with ethnicity from the census because of the matching of the census data with voters and with ICRC records of the missing persons. So once these records -- I am speaking records, individual level records describing cases were matched, it was possible to transfer information from the census records onto either voters records or missing persons records. So that was the major thing in our methodology, using, one, the same definition of ethnicity for pre and post-war period, and using the definition that was coming from this open-ended question from the population census.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Page 13. Could you please explain how you identified who was an internally displaced person, an IDP, and who was a refugee, briefly if possible?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Identifying IDPs and refugees was based on a statistical approach and not on a legal approach, so our statistical -- in our statistical approach an IDP, internally displaced person, was a person who resided in the post-conflict period at a different municipality than was reported for the person in the population census. So in order to decide who is displaced, who is not, we simply compared the place of residence of individuals as reported before the conflict in '91 population census on one hand and voters registers for the post-conflict period as a proxy for the residents, post-war residents, the municipality of registration was taken. And the same with refugees with the difference that refugees were not the persons who moved within the borders of Bosnia and Herzegovina but left the country and moved abroad.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Page 14. In your expert report you refer to minimum numbers. Could you explain briefly, please, what is meant by the term "minimum numbers"?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: So minimum numbers are the numbers that were produced based on the matched records. So whoever was reported in the voters and was back traced in '91 records in the census is a matched record and using these matched records it was possible to produce the so-called minimum numbers, the minimum or at least numbers. All these numbers can be documented individually, that means by attaching lists of persons with names and other details, but we know for sure these lists are an underestimation, undercount. I shouldn't say estimation, because it is not an estimate, it is a count, a count, a statistic produced from data, individual data. So in order to work with these numbers of course these are good statistics based on solid data from large sample, but we know they are not complete, they are incomplete, and we can explain why by using other sources, for instance, UNHCR for instance reported many more internally displaced than what we show in this report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I'd like to please skip page 15 and go to page 16. Dr. Tabeau, could you please explain what the chart on the top of this page represents.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: This is a table coming from the report, table 3A from page 30 English version. This table is showing ethnic composition in the Visegrad municipality. Both absolute numbers and percentages are shown. The '91 census column contains statistics, counts coming from the census data. This is the population of those eligible to vote in the 1997 and 1998 elections so this is why this number, the overall total is smaller than the general total for Visegrad as published in official sources. The next column is a sample data coming from the voters registration. So this is the overall total 9.241 is not the size, overall size of the 1997 population. It is just a large sample from this population. We show these numbers by ethnicity, major findings in terms of percentages which are good and reliable measures. Disregarding whether they were obtained from the census data or voters registration that is sample data so the percentages can be safely taken as reliable measures of ethnic composition, and we see for instance, that the per cent of Serbs in 1991 was about 32.6 per cent and increased according to the voters registration in 1997 to approximately 95.9 per cent. For Muslims it was a slightly different situation. From a 62.5 per cent it dropped to almost 0, less than 1 per cent. And so on for every ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can you look at the bottom of the page, please, and tell us what conclusions can be drawn from this chart at the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: This bar chart illustrates the percentages from the table 3A shown on the same page. Each ethnic group is shown separately. For the Serbs we see a huge increase of the fraction of Serbs in the municipality. For the Muslims a dramatic drop from about 63 per cent to practically 0. So the Muslim population shown in this chart is almost entirely gone from Visegrad. This is what this bar chart is showing.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Page 17. Dr. Tabeau, could you briefly tell us what this chart represents and what conclusions we can draw from it?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, this table again comes from the report. This is table 3B. The table 3B from page 13 in the report consists of two parts. I'm only showing the part with percentages. I'm not showing absolute numbers, but the 3B with absolute numbers is in the report. The table shown here should be read by rows. For each ethnicity a distribution is shown of the post-conflict place of residence of this ethnic group. The first group, the Serbs, are shown in the post-conflict period as mainly residing still in the municipality of Visegrad. So I'm speaking of 96.9 per cent in the first row. Given under the name this municipality. So this municipality means that these are those from the initial population, 1991 population reported in the census who didn't move anywhere but just stayed in Visegrad. So according to this table, 96.9 per cent stayed, of Serbs stayed in Visegrad. So automatically the percentages of those who have been reported in other municipalities in Bosnia or other countries are extremely small. Other municipalities is less than 1 per cent, and the out of country 2.2 per cent. For Muslims the picture is quite opposite. In these municipalities it is negligible value of 0.01 per cent reported in Visegrad in the post-conflict period, and the rest, that is 99.9 per cent of the Muslim population originating from Visegrad is reported either in other municipalities in Bosnia or generally out of country. And similarly the percentage of other groups is shown according to the distribution by place of residence being the Visegrad or outside Visegrad, but to generalise, to summarise this picture I can say that generally 65 per cent of the pre-war population of Visegrad had become displaced or left the country, 65 per cent, all ethnicities jointly. Of all ethnicities, Muslims practically entirely left the municipality. Of other non-Serbs, some Croats and others stayed, some left. Generally about 63 per cent of non-Serbs left Visegrad as well. That would be a majority. And of course the first issue -- the first result I discussed, the Serbs, 97 per cent of Serbs stayed in Visegrad. This had, of course, impact on the post-war ethnic composition in the municipality. Those Serbs who stayed plus some newcomers, obviously Serbs, resulted in the fact that in 1997 the municipality was dominated by Serbs, had an absolute majority, large majority of the Serb population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks very much, Dr. Tabeau. We have to take the break now.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: These two charts come from the second part of the report in which the numbers of missing persons from the Visegrad municipality and Visegrad region were studied. utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I think Dr. Tabeau would like to use the ELMO, and she's pointing with her pen, so ...

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: As I said, missing persons reported missing from the Visegrad municipalities are shown here by the month of disappearance for the entire conflict period starting with April 1992 until the last one shown is August 1995. That would be the first chart, the upper chart. And there is the lower chart. So having shown that the largest number of missing persons was in the spring and summer of 1992, the lower chart is showing the distribution of going missing by date of disappearance from April 1992 until end of June 1992. The 15th of May is somewhere here. So starting from this day the numbers are clearly high, higher and highest. So second half of May is the first period of obviously increased activity of -- of the process of going missing, and then the June until the 20th of June and the last days of June. So sometime around May 25th, June 14th, and June 20th, these three days, are local maxima where the numbers were the highest in this period.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. The following block is variables called voters and DDPR. These are sources reporting on the surviving population --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I apologise. Can you confirm that if the Trial Chamber or the Defence has any questions about any individual entries on this chart you would be able to provide those clarifications?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, in relation to both these charts that we've just had marked for identification, can you talk briefly about the dates and any accuracy or inaccuracy, reliability of the dates of death or the dates of disappearance?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, dates is a data item that is difficult for the respondent to remember exactly. So it often happens that dates are reported not fully correctly or not fully completely. So with the ICRC list for instance there is a about say 30 per cent in the 2005 edition of date of birth that is not available as a complete item with all components, day and month and year reported, but when it comes to the year of birth then there is only a few in the entire list of 22.000 records that are unavailable, like 10, 12 records don't include year of birth. But generally it is not only the ICRC list. In many sources, especially sources that were compiled without using any ID cards or passports or any documents reporting the date of birth, black on white, dates are not reported correctly. And especially if data is collected in chaotic circumstances or an in a situation just after certain dramatic events, then this has of course impact on the reporting quality and then certain deficiencies can be also seen in the dates. I am speaking of date of birth, but the same actually applies to the date of disappearance or date of death. Many sources with which we have to work were compiled by not non-professionals, not by statisticians, just by NGOs or volunteers who wanted to share the information they had with somebody. These dates are reported simply with deficiencies, either incomplete or with certain errors. So when cross-referencing sources it is often the case that we see small differences in the date of birth or the date of disappearance or death.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Tabeau. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Marcus. Well, we've heard the submissions that were made by --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON

utterances.text: Your Honour, I think our plans can be adjusted since we have not been able to talk to Ms. Tabeau or Dr. Tabeau, could I ask the Court to inquire if -- I know that she had some annual leave planned in the near future, if we could ask, inquire if she's available on Wednesday for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Your are available on --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm unavailable from Friday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- until Monday, but Wednesday, Thursday I'm in, I am available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I believe we would complete the cross-examination on Wednesday certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I will make the necessary adjustments to the schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In that case, Dr. Tabeau, we would discharge you for the time being.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have another witness, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, Dr. John Clark is in the waiting-room. Your Honour, while we're waiting the witness if I might address the Chamber on a brief matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I read the Chamber's decision with respect to VG-42 and take note of the Chamber finding unacceptable that the Prosecution had brought the witness to The Hague. I just want to state to the Chamber it was not anticipate -- in anticipation of any particular ruling by the Chamber but simply trying to -- to keep the court hearing days fully occupied. We are getting to a stage now in the trial where we have less of a pool of witnesses to call upon, so I apologise to the Chamber if the Chamber thought that we were anticipating -- or I was anticipating a decision by the Chamber, simply an effort to ensure that there was no gaps in the hearing time. I would also raise with the Chamber there are pending motions with respect to a number of witnesses. I have asked, again in an effort to ensure that the hearing schedule not be postponed, and I'm also aware that sometimes passports take up to three weeks to obtain. I have asked staff to work with these witnesses to get their passports. If the Chamber finds that objectionable, I will certainly cease that practice and await the Chamber's ruling on these witnesses. Again it's not to anticipate a particular ruling by the Chamber but simply if the Chamber does decide to permit the inclusion of these witnesses that there will be a minimum of delay between the time that -- that is necessary to make the necessary arrangements for them to come to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In the circumstances I find the practice unobjectionable. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm just taking advantage of these couple of minutes and I would like to ask my friends from the OTP to disclose and hand over to us documents in a timelier manner from now on in order to make our work in the courtroom more effective. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, you have been rebuked.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit, and you may begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Ms. Mazzocco will lead the examination in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may begin, Ms. Mazzocco.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: Can I first ask you to say your name, please?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: John Clark.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, can you describe to the Court your education, your profession, in particular the assignment you received in an international context?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: My profession, I'm a forensic pathologist. That means I'm a medical doctor, and I specialise in finding out why people have died by carrying out post-mortem examinations, particularly with a forensic expertise it is interpreting injuries on bodies and dealing with people who have died in perhaps suspicious circumstances. I've been a forensic pathologist for about 25 years working both in -- mainly in -- well, in the United Kingdom, both in Scotland where I'm based at the moment and in England as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: And you have worked in international context, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: My main contribution to that has been this work with which I'm here. For three years, 1999, 2000, and 2001 I was the chief pathologist in Bosnia and Croatia for the ICTY carrying out the -- in charge of the mortuary there and carrying out the post-mortem examinations.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: May I ask the court officer to display on the screen the 65 ter number 2.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Where are you from, doctor? Where are you from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Where are you from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm from Glasgow. University of Glasgow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Glasgow. You're Scottish then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm Scottish, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, is this your updated CV, the one that you see on the screen?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, it is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender the CV into evidence to the purpose to determining the witness former and present position and the professional experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We admit it, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is admitted as P121, Exhibit P121.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, you have said that you participate as chief pathologist to the ICTY operation in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Which were the years?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: We have heard evidence that many people were killed in Visegrad area. Could you examine all the victims?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: I'm not aware of how many people were killed in the Visegrad area. I understand that there were large numbers. Our -- my only involvement in -- in that region was dealing with a specific site, what we called the Slap site of 131 bodies. This was a specific exercise which we did in 2000 -- late 2000 and again in 2001.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: Did you work together with a Bosnian commission?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. Slightly unusually because most of the work that we had been doing, the Tribunal did both the exhumation and the mortuary work in other cases. In this instance, the Slap site, it was people from the Bosnian commission who did the exhumation and they formally handed over the bodies to us and we carried out -- the Tribunal carried out the post-mortem examinations. And following that, we handed the bodies back over to the Bosnian commission.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: Who signed each autopsy report?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: The -- at any one time there would be three pathologists in the mortuary carrying out the post-mortem examination simultaneously. So we had three tables. And the pathologist carrying out the examination would have signed the autopsy report. Having said that, there was a lot of discussion between us in each cases and we showed each other findings. So although one person may have signed the report, the others will have often have seen the findings as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: You have said that you have -- you found in the -- you studied 131 bodies. What was the sex and age of these bodies?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: I don't have my report with me, but the -- I think a hundred and -- about 114 were male. May I have a copy of the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: Yes, yes. If you have -- can I ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. You may look at the report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The majority were male. I can tell you that. Yes. 114. This is of 131 bodies, 114 were male, 14 were female, and in three cases we were unable to determine the sex, and these were mostly young people.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: Were the bodies numbered?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. The Bosnian commission had numbered the bodies as they exhumed them, and they gave them a number. For some reason they started at number 317. I'm not quite sure the reason for that, but anyway, when they handed the bodies over and during our examination, we continued that numbering system, and we put letters at the beginning and at the end to denote the site we were working on and whether this was a body or -- there was only one instance where there was a body part. So the numbering system that we used followed on from the numbering system from the Bosnian commission.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: Can you describe the main difficulties you related to this type of autopsy work?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: All these bodies were skeletonised. In other words, we were -- all the soft tissues of the body had disappeared and all that we were left with were just the skeleton, and the bones were jumbled in together. So there wasn't a straight skeleton, they were mixed in together, in with clothing and sometimes various other items in with the body. So that's what we had to deal with, skeletonised remains. Now, our job was to try and find any injuries on these people and try and establish the cause of death. So all we could work on were any injuries to the bones. That's what we had to work on. So if somebody had been injured in a way which didn't damage the bones, we wouldn't have seen that. Also, we had to bear in mind that injuries can occur to bones of the bodies after death, and it is very difficult just looking at bones themselves to see whether an injury occurred in life or after death. So we had to keep a very open mind, and it was quite likely that there would be injuries to these bodies after death -- to the bones after death because they had been in a grave, just handling, et cetera. But with experience we were able to recognise what was likely to be a post-mortem injury and what was not. Anyway, so that was one of the main problems; we were left with bones and to try and establish whether these injuries on them occurred in life or after death. Secondly was having found an injury, trying to work out what caused it. Was this a bullet injury? Was this caused by blunt force injuries, blunt force trauma, in other words, being hit by something or was it caused by a knife or whatever. So that was the other task we had to do. And thirdly, even having found an injury, even having established that it was due to a gunshot injury or whatever, could we then see that was necessarily the cause of death because people don't die from a broken bone. You die because of the injuries to all the organs round about, the internal tissues. So because we only had bones and even though there was a bone -- an injury in the bone, could we necessarily say that that's what killed that person. So -- so there was lots of -- there were difficulties in the interpretation, and we had to bear that in mind all the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: And so how did you prove an injury as being due to gunshot as opposed to other causes?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: When a bullet hits bone, it causes characteristic damage, particularly with a high velocity rifle. It shatters the bone. It causes a huge amount of damage. So many of the bones that we saw were in -- in lots of pieces, different pieces, but with the aid of the anthropologists, we were able to stick these together and -- and perhaps find actually a hole with lots of fracturing round about it. And if we found that, then we were fairly convinced that this was a gunshot injury. And often there would be bullet fragments in the body as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: Sorry. Was it possible to determine whether it was a high velocity rifle was used or a handgun?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Nearly all of the cases the pattern of injuries, the nature of the damage to the bones was very typical of high velocity injuries. The reason for that is if you fire a handgun a handgun will damage a bone just simply by the hole it produces. So if you have a bone and a handgun bullet goes through the bone, it just creates a hole. But a high velocity rifle, it creates not just a hole but a huge amount of fracturing round about, and because -- it was because of this extensive fracturing we could say the vast majority of cases were high velocity rifles. We did in two cases find handgun bullets and injuries pointing to that which very much suggested that these people had been killed by handguns rather than high velocity rifles. That was the exception. The vast majority were the high velocity rifles.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: Thank you. And were you able to determine the direction of fire, the position between the victim and the attacker?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: To some extent but not in all cases. That is based on again if a bullet goes through bone, particularly the skull or a rib it leaves a characteristic pattern or shape from which you can tell the direction it's going. So, for instance, if a bullet entered the back of the head and came out the front, we could tell the direct just by the shape of the bone if you look at the outside and the inside surface, and it's highly typical, well documented. So most times with the skull it was easy to tell that. It's less easy on other bones. And in the end we could only tell direction in a certain proportion, but -- and this is listed in the -- in the report. For instance, of all the shots -- of all the shots to the head, just -- the majority were from behind or the side and lesser numbers from the front and occasionally from the top. So I think to answer your question, there was variable -- the bullets were fired in variable directions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: In -- in which phase of this process were the bodies shown to the families for possible identification?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: That was after our official involvement. Although our main role was to look at injuries and establish cause of death, we did as much as we could as well to aid identification by taking measurements of the skeleton, seeing it was male or female, all that sort of stuff, looking for documents and photographing the clothing, et cetera, documenting that. With that information we handed that all over to the Bosnian commission, and I'm aware that they then showed the clothing and the remains and documents to relatives to try and seek some identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Sorry, just one other thing. We also took from each body a sample of bone for future DNA analysis. DNA analysis on bone in that time, even only seven years ago, was in its infancy and it wasn't really possible or practical to do DNA analysis then. That has changed now and in recent years a lot of analysis, DNA analysis has been done.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: Could I ask the court officer to display the screen the document bearing the 65 ter number 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, is this the report that you signed as chief pathologist and that summarises the finding from the Slap grave sites?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. The -- what happened here was after all the post-mortems, the 131 post-mortems compiled by myself, my colleagues, I extracted the information from them and made this final report which is what you have now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender the report into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is admitted as Exhibit P122, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: And may I now ask the court officer to display page 10 of this 65 ter number 1, the same. And maybe can figure 6 at the top be enlarged. The one on the left.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: Can you explain the findings of this photograph that come from autopsy report 361?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: This is -- the bone at the top there is the shoulder blade, the scapula. Down below it we have five ribs laid out like that. Now, this is not the normal anatomical position. This is just for ease of photographing. So you can imagine the ribs effectively lying on top of the shoulder blade. Now, what this does show, however, is a hole in the shoulder blade, in the middle of it. You can just see the blue coming through it where there's an arrow pointing to it. And if you go down a bit further down you will see holes in the ribs, a line of holes. Now, that to us was a typical pattern of a gunshot, of a bullet going through the body, and although I've listed five holes that you can see, that is probably all the same track because of where the ribs are against the shoulder blade. So that's a typical bullet going through the upper part of the trunk.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: Can the court officer display the document bearing number X008/0291. Should I repeat maybe? X008/0291. This one. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: Is this the autopsy report related to body 361?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: And the one related to that photo that we have seen now. And in this case was it possible to determine the cause of death?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: The cause of death we attributed was that bullet injury, the gunshot injury to the chest. I explained earlier that all we found there is a bullet to the bone, but I think, you know, as pathologists we know that under the shoulder blade under the ribs you have the major organs. You have the lungs and the heart, et cetera, and I think it's reasonable to suggest that these -- these parts of the body would have been injured and fatally so and that this -- this was the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: And was it possible in this case to determine the direction of fire?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Perhaps if you went down a page. It's page 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: I read it in this page.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Oh, yes, sorry, yes. The shot was coming -- seemed to be coming from behind. Sorry. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to tender this document into evidence. And can I now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is admitted Exhibit P number 123.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: Can I now ask the court officer to display the document bearing number 0638/3236.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: Do you recognise the number at the top of the page on the right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: The number is almost certainly the same numbering system that we used, 361/00. I have no reason to believe that any new numbering system was used, so I think that applies to the body that we saw.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: So can you explain the process related to this document? Was --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: I -- this -- we handed the bodies over to the Bosnian commission, and that -- that was the end of our involvement. I'm aware, just because I was in the area at the time, that they had an identification process soon afterwards and that relatives were invited to come and look at the clothing and possessions, as I said earlier, and I can only imagine that as relatives did identify to their purposes each body that this form was produced by the Bosnian commission. But it's not an official form from anything that we did, but -- but I just -- I'm aware of the process that went on. I think that's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P124, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: Can I now ask the court officer to display the document with number X007/7947.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, can you describe what you see on the screen?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: This is another autopsy report, SP01/378B which was carried out in May 2001.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: And so is -- which body is related? You said, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: And in this case was it possible to determine the cause of death?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. He again died from a gunshot injury to the chest.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is admitted as number -- Exhibit number P125.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: And finally can I ask the court officer to display the document with number X007/9454.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, is this the autopsy report your team drafted concerned the body 328?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, this is SP01/328B carried out in November 2000, and I felt that this man probably died from a gunshot injury to the chest. This was a little less definite than the previous two but there appeared to be bullet damage to three ribs on the right side of the chest and there were bullet holes in the clothing that he was wearing. So I felt the most probable cause of death was a gunshot injury to the chest.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's admitted as Exhibit number P126.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Are we going to do cross, it's 7.00, tonight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We do go on --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Until 7.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. Ten past 7.00. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Ten past 7.00, okay. I forget these things, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, from your data at Slap would it be fair to say that none of the bodies originated there at Slap; this was not an execution site. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Not as far as I'm aware, no. These were all bodies buried in individual graves which we understood floated down the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you got that understanding from third-party sources, but was that an exhaustive assessment of the location of the body or is it possible that some others were brought there from other locales as opposed to the river?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: That's entirely possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say there was very little information as to where on the river or otherwise the bodies were actually killed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could speakers please kindly pause between questions and answers for the benefit of the interpreters, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Have you both heard that? Please observe a pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour, and I didn't have my translation headset on because I can hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so it is possible that the -- or you can't tell from the locale where exactly the body was deceased; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And just by virtue of your role, you didn't have any participation in the actual family identification. Is that what I heard?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: None at all, no. I was -- it was done in the same areas where we were working, and I saw it as an interested observer, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And with regards to the actual bodies, you indicated it was -- well, it appears from the documentation that you just used it was even difficult to assess the age in some.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. The age was established not by us but by anthropologists, who gave the information to us, but even they would give a range of -- of years, you know, 20 to 30 years sometimes as a range of age. It is very difficult in general principles to establish somebody's age from bones the older you get.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And it appears from -- from your findings that the grave site in and of itself was fairly disorganised?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't -- certainly not from our findings. I thought it was to some extent remarkably well organised. I did visit it after the exhumation, and I understand that the graves were -- they were largely individual graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Was there some contamination, i.e., bodies being too close together or mishandled at the scene, because it appears that you had some partial skeletons recovered. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: That's right. I didn't witness the exhumation process. There may have been some transferring of occasional bones, I do not know. I think it would be wrong for me to say there was mishandling.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, I mean under the -- you know, under the worst of circumstances there might have been mistakes made with regards to the handling of the corpses?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: I think other people should answer that. I mean, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: How many people would you say could have handled a particular corpse before you get to do your analysis?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: I would imagine maybe perhaps two or three people were involved in exhuming each particular body, which would be put into a body bag, and after that the body bag would not be opened until I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Even with respect to the body bag, you said that the remains were all skeletonised?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Is it true that you were getting incomplete skeletons?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: A number of the bodies did have parts missing, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And would you assume that that was because the bodies were dismembered at another locale or that there was actually mishandling at the grave site?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: No. There could be various reasons, and I put this in the context of having been involved in other grave sites by highly experienced exhumation teams, even there we would get small parts of other bodies in with other cases. I think there's possibly three reasons why parts of bodies may be missing. Firstly, if this was just -- quite a lot of time it was just the small bones of the hands and the wrist. They are very difficult to find, and they were probably just left in the soil. Secondly, yes, you're correct. In taking a body out of the grave it is possible that occasionally parts ended up in the wrong body bag. I don't know. I'm just raising it as a possibility. And the third possibility is that prior to burial these bodies were missing a particular part. A limb wasn't present prior to burial. I cannot tell what state the body was in prior to burial, whether they were decomposed or fresh or whatever, and it's possible with a very decomposed body that parts were missing prior to burial.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And even with regards to trying to assess bullet direction, would it be fair to say that absent the soft tissue you can make mistakes simply because a high velocity bullet absent intervention can even cause a nice circular hole in bone at the exit wound?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: I'm not sure I follow that completely but --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, on the scapula you indicated that that was most probably a rear shot?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But on the same token it is possible for that pattern in the scapula at least to have been caused from a frontal shot?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: It is possible. I mean, even in the scapula they do have -- what we're looking for is a thing called bevelling. In other words, the diameter of the hole on the entrance side is smaller than the diameter hole on the exit side of the bone, and that's typically seen in the skull and it can occur to see it in the ribs and in the scapula. I can't remember in this particular case how definite that direction was, but certainly with the ribs, taking the ribs into account as well, I think we were confident that this shot was coming from behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Arguing that the ribs were deflective of damage on the exit wound? Meaning that they were getting the deflective energy as the bullet travelled outwards?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: No, no, the ribs were -- it would have hit the ribs first.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry. It hit the scapula first and then the ribs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: That's what I thought.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. Would it be fair to say otherwise that some of these wounds could have been achieved in combat? I.e., there is no real way to tell whether or not there was a civilian casualty or an actual combat casualty?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: No, not from the pathology evidence, no. I can't -- I cannot tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I have no further questions at this time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cepic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How long are you going to be?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: I have less than 20 questions and it takes 15 minutes perhaps 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think we'll have to do that tomorrow then. We will adjourn. Doctor, you will have to return tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Tomorrow it's at -- in the afternoon, 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 23rd day of September, 2008, at 2.15 p.m.
